# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# What the follow-up reports

This report combines two 24-month follow-ups, co-authored by the Varden team and one of the Halden authors.

**Varden case-processing (7 v 7 offices, randomised schedules kept for two years):**

- Output per employee: −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2).
- Actual hours: −12% on timesheets, −11% on a new system-log measure.
- Output per hour: +9.8% on timesheets and +8.5% on logs, against +12.5% on timesheets at nine months. Quality is unchanged.
- Mediation analysis, registered at month 11: meetings explain 47% of the per-hour gain, fatigue 18%, and 35% is unexplained.
- Two control offices cut meetings on their own in month 15. Their output per hour then rose 4.1% against their own previous six months.

**Varden counter arm:** the county ended it at month 12. Waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and restoring service would have needed 12% more staff.

**Halden (14 of the 23 organisations with output records responded):**

- Three reverted, at record-based output of 88–91.
- The 11 that continued show output 96.8 and hours −13.4%, so about +11.8% per hour. The authors present this as an upper bound for organisations that self-select and find the schedule suits them.

**Responses to the earlier documents:** the authors argue that "entirely an artifact" fails the re-analysis's own standards. They report that the meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, so they cannot speak to decay.

**Arithmetic.** All figures check:

- 0.966/0.88 = +9.8%
- 0.966/0.89 = +8.5%
- 34.9/40.3 = −13.4%
- 96.8/0.866 = +11.8%
- 47 + 18 + 35 = 100
- Meetings: −3.5 hours in treated offices against −0.2 in control offices, consistent with the month-six figures in the nine-month report.

# What this settles

Several points can now be treated as closed.

**"Entirely an artifact" is refuted for this setting.** The Varden 24-month result meets the standards the re-analysis itself recommended: randomised comparison, record-based output, actual hours, and well over 18 months. It finds +8.5% with an interval that clearly excludes zero.

**"No sign of decay" in the meta-analysis can't stand.** The four long studies have exactly the design features the meta-analysis showed inflate effects. This confirms the earlier suspicion.

**The counter arm is now a properly controlled result.** Waits are compared with control offices, and there is a staffing-cost estimate. The coverage-bound conclusion is firmer than before.

**The timesheet worry was small.** On logs, hours fell by 11% rather than 12%.

**The 11 continuing Halden organisations are framed correctly.** Calling their figure an upper bound for self-selecting survivors is the right weight to give it.

# Where the report overstates

**1. The size of the decline mixes two measures, and the decline itself isn't tested.**

The summary's "12.5% to 8.5%" compares nine-month timesheets with 24-month logs. Like for like, the change is 12.5% to 9.8%, about a fifth. Section 3 does this correctly, but the summary and Section 5's "about a quarter" lean on the mixed comparison.

More importantly, the change is never estimated. The nine-month and 24-month intervals overlap heavily (6.9 to 18.4 against 4.6 to 15.2). "The gain has declined" therefore isn't established, and the data are also consistent with no decline.

With only two time points, a plateau and continued slow decay also can't be told apart. Monthly data exist, so the trajectory and a test of the change should be shown. Until then:

- the gain persisting at a lower level is settled;
- how fast it decays, and whether it stabilises, is open.

The re-analysis was partly right on direction, which the report fairly acknowledges with "some fading".

**2. The mediation result "confirms" more than this design can deliver.**

Registering the analysis removes analytic flexibility. But it uses the same seven treated offices whose correlation (r = 0.71) prompted the hypothesis. A "larger sample of office-months" adds repeated measurements of those same offices, not independent ones. This is a pre-specified re-test, not a replication on new units.

The intervals (28 to 66, 2 to 34) also likely carry the small-cluster problem noted for the nine-month report, since there are 14 clusters.

Mediation further assumes no unmeasured confounding. Meeting cuts were chosen by managers, so better managers might both cut meetings and raise output. The limitations concede this, yet the summary says "confirms."

The finding is now well supported in direction, a substantial step up from exploratory. The 47% share should be stated as an estimate under that assumption, not as a measured fact. "Supports" would be accurate where the summary says "confirms."

**3. The control offices' meeting audit needs a comparison, and may count as contamination.**

The +4.1% is a before-and-after comparison within those two offices. It should be set against the trend in the other five control offices over the same period.

Control offices copying a practice from treated offices is also spillover between arms. It is small and would bias toward zero, but it should be noted. The report's handling of the hours-versus-reorganisation question is otherwise exactly right: that question is open, and no arm can answer it.

# Questions about definitions and data

**What does log time include?** If it records only time "working on cases", it probably excludes meetings. In that case:

- "Output per log-measured hour" is output per hour of case work, a different quantity from output per hour worked. It is not simply a "stricter" version of the same measure.
- The meetings mediation then means something specific: fewer meetings make case-time itself more productive, perhaps through less fragmentation. Cutting meetings would not just remove unproductive hours from the denominator.

Both readings are interesting, but they matter differently for employers. The definition should be stated.

**Where did the baseline meeting data come from?** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. The baseline figures here (7.4 and 7.2 hours) suggest calendars were retrieved retrospectively. That is fine if so, but the report should say so, because the difference-in-differences on meeting time depends on it.

**Which period does "24 months" cover?** If it averages the whole period, the comparison with nine months understates any later decline. If it covers only the last stretch, the report should say which months.

# The Halden subset

**Non-response.** Nine of the 23 organisations did not respond. Non-responders are plausibly enriched for reverters, so 3 of 14 is likely a lower bound on reversion.

**The reversion category is stretched.** "All with client-facing or coverage obligations" covers a marketing agency that cited client deadlines. That is a discretionary-sector organisation, and widening the category to fit it after the fact weakens the dichotomy. It is better reported plainly: one of the three reversions was in discretionary work.

**The attrition finding goes unanswered.** Section 5 addresses the re-analysis's conclusion but not its finding that the working paper misreported when and why nine organisations withdrew. With a Halden author on this report, acknowledging or correcting that point belongs here.

# Still outstanding from earlier reports

- **Backlog and time to decision.** The nine-month limitations raised whether backlogs build beyond statutory deadlines. Twenty-four months is when to report it, and nothing is reported.
- **Small-cluster inference.** Wild-cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference has still not been reported.
- **Office-specific queues.** Whether case queues and call routing are separate for each office, the spillover question, is still unanswered.
- **Sick days per scheduled day.** The −27% may still partly arise from fewer scheduled days.

# Where things stand now

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Headline per-hour gains above 20% are inflated | Settled |
| Per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" | Refuted for discretionary public-sector work |
| A per-hour gain persists at 24 months in discretionary work | Supported: about 8.5–10%, randomised, one employer |
| The gain has declined since nine months | Point estimate lower. The change is untested, and its rate and endpoint are open |
| Output per employee in discretionary work | Slightly below control. A loss of up to about 8% is not excluded |
| Coverage-bound work: output and service fall, restoring them costs staff | Well supported. The employer abandoned the arm |
| Meetings as a mechanism | Well supported in direction under a pre-specified test. Size depends on the no-confounding assumption, and the test used the same units |
| Gains available without cutting hours | Open. Suggestive evidence from two offices. Needs an arm that reorganises without reducing hours |
| Long-run durability beyond two years | Open |
| Generalisation to private-sector work and manufacturing | Open |

The study that would settle the biggest remaining question is a three-arm trial: reduced hours, a meeting and process audit at unchanged hours, and control. That comparison would show whether the hours cut matters itself, or mainly forces a reorganisation that could happen without it. I can sketch that design, or draft review comments on this report.
